items.title: An ethical AI does not exist
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

Credit: USDA NRCS Montana Flickr

I’ve been seeing more and more arguments from people who are nominally anti-AI, but deftly clarify that they are only against generative AI “in its current form” or “as it is deployed today” (I confess that I used to be part of that group years ago). Statements like that imply that there exists a good and ethical way to create and deploy AI, such that its use becomes ethically free from major concern. There’s only one problem: No one has actually described what such an ethical AI would look like, or how it would be built or deployed.

The problems plaguing AI today are numerous and well-documented . Everything in the AI pipeline—the theft of content, the abuse of training labor, the energy consumption, the scandalous financing, the psychological harms, the pollution of the commons—is problematic and harmful. How much of that pipeline would one have to change to make the development and use of a new AI ethically acceptable?

Reading these essays, I understand the rage the author expresses. It's hard not to see your own body's actions as some form of betrayal, and it's even harder to develop warm feelings towards the aids that help with functionality. Especially with how the people around you can treat you…

items.title: Walking the length of the Harringay Passage
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

Harringay – Turnpike Lane – Hornsey – Parkland Walk North – Alexandra Palace

I summoned this walk from a sketch in my Morning Pages . Trying to work out where to go I drew an outline of London that appeared like a sigil which conjured a mile-long alley running parallel to Green Lanes, Harringay. I’d thought about walking the Harringay Passage from end to end since I lived on the Harringay Ladder in my last year of Poly, but never got round to it. Now I found myself looking down its length from Umfreville Road and off I set.

Passing stink pipes, schools, and the baffling naming sequence of the streets on the Harringay Ladder, I emerged on Turnpike Lane so disoriented I failed to notice that the spelling had changed from Harringay Passage to Haringey Passage. I pushed on up into deepest darkest Hornsey looking for the start of the next pathway.

It’s unfortunate to say the least that Parkland Walk North starts too close to the site of Dennis Nilsen’s horrific crimes…

items.title: The message is not for you
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
Often, when someone appears to be speaking to you, they are actually speaking to themselves. Their soul is persistent in getting them to hear what they are avoiding in themselves, and in trying to slip the message across the subject of what is being said can become diffused, increasingly so the longer the person has been avoiding themselves. So when you hear something absurd, cruel, disrespectful, violent, profuse, intense, emphatic, fiercely enthusiastic - consider that you are eavesdropping. Consider that the message is not for you.

Being able to tell the difference between when someone is speaking to you and when they are speaking to themselves (these can co-exist in varying proportions) is key.

items.title: 《如何阅读一棵树》part_3
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
树的顶芽分泌生长素，这种生长素会抑制下层树枝的生长。针叶树的生长素对下层树枝生长抑制更严重，针叶林形态更呈现圆锥形（当然还有其他因素，但生长素是主因），而阔叶树生长素对下层树枝抑制一般，阔叶树形态常呈现球形。

一旦去掉顶芽（可能是大风、或者是动物啃咬等），下面的树枝会快速生长，长出新的树枝，这种生存机制允许一棵树在经历“灭顶之灾”后改变策略，重新生长，这是形之有效的策略。

农业种植的时候，也会利用这个特性，比如对高度足够，长出果实的棉花植株进行“去顶”，从而促进果实生长。还有对作为篱笆的植物“去顶”，让篱笆的侧枝生长更稠密。

Sergeant Nessilka leads her troop in an attack, only for things to go.… wrong. She does not get paid enough for this.

Short, and quite sweet. I enjoyed the various characters, and world-building well enough, but found the story itself a little lacking. I’d have liked a little more meat, but there is only so much space in a novella.

The author’s note at the end reveals this is an updated version of her first foray into self-published fiction for adults, and the feel of the writing suddenly made more sense. While Nine Goblins is a fun, fast read Kingfisher has definitely levelled up as a writer since then.

Nearly nine years ago on this website I took a dive into the Marxist concept of Basis und Überbau, 'Base and the Superstructure'. This concept – arguably one of the most profound, subtle and useful ideas that Marx came up with – has been largely ignored by his followers, who, it seems, have been more interested in fomenting unrest and revolution than doing a bit of deep thinking.

The ignorance and stupidity of the GenZ kids currently demonstrating in support of their demands took me back those nine years.

Marx's insight can be stated very simply. The means of production form the base on which the culture of a society rests. Loosely rephrased in modern, non-Marxist terminology: the technologies available in our society determine our culture (in the very broadest sense of that word, including the way we think and the way we speak).

items.title: Preparing the earth for a persimmon tree
items.label: Q&A

I have an enormous aloe plant (about 6 feet tall, 5 feet across) that we are taking out and replacing with a persimmon tree. I'm wondering if there is something we should do between the aloe coming out and the tree going in to prepare the earth to make the tree more likely to succeed.

Given the size of the aloe, I'm expecting that it'll have a pretty big root structure that we won't be able to get access to (there is cement around 1/2 of the planting area). We have chickens and could set them up in the spot to turn over the earth after the aloe comes out. We could add compost, plant a temporary cover crop, just let it rest for a season to give the roots time to decompose, or just put the persimmon tree in right away and hope for the best.

Where I live doesn't hit freezing, but does get a lot of rain in the winter.

Any thoughts on how to prepare the earth for the new tree?

items.title: Small portion of damaged gutter = replace the entire house's gutters??
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
Part of a tree fell on my parents' roof, damaging a portion of gutter. A gutter installer says that the only right way to fix this is to replace the gutters all the way around the house. Can that possibly be right? Details below.

The tree didn't damage the roofing itself, but it did cause some of the gutter to get a little bent up and detached from the roof. The damaged area happens to include a downspout and occurs at a roof corner. I reckon about 3' to 5' of gutter length on each side of the corner (so maybe 8' total length) is affected.
